statements.section: Proposition H - Parcel Tax to Fund Public Muni Operations
statements.text: Prop H would introduce a parcel tax from 2027-2042 to assist in funding San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency operations. The anticipated revenue generated from this tax would be about $177 million. The Chamber supports Prop H as public transit is a critical driver of the San Francisco economy, helping workers, residents, and businesses stay connected.

statements.section: Mayor Lurie Joined by Firefighters and Police Officers in Strong Opposition to Proposition I
statements.text: The timing of the special-interest led Proposition I could not be worse. San Francisco is in the middle of its most aggressive first-responder hiring push in years.

statements.section: Govern For California, San Francisco Chapter, November 2026 Voter Guide
statements.text: The San Francisco Chapter supports capable leaders, responsible fiscal management, effective public services, affordability, public safety, and policies that promote San Francisco's long-term economic competitiveness.

statements.kind: voter guide on the organisation's own site
statements.section: Proposition J, Foreclosure Transfer Tax: NO
statements.text: San Francisco's commercial real estate market is already under tremendous stress, and adding transfer taxes to foreclosures and distressed property workouts would make matters worse. The city should be encouraging capital to return to its struggling real estate market, not making it more expensive to invest.

statements.kind: voter guide on the organisation's own site
statements.section: Proposition C, Affordable Housing Trust Fund: YES
statements.text: San Francisco's housing costs are already too high, and imposing expensive requirements on private development only makes the problem worse. Prop C preserves a compromise that reduces certain inclusionary housing requirements in exchange for greater direct funding of affordable housing, without creating a new tax.

statements.kind: advocacy page on the organisation's own site
statements.text: The SFAA's Political Action Committee (SFAA PAC) supports candidates for local political office like the SF School Board, the Board of Supervisors and Mayor, the City Attorney, state representatives, and more. SFAA's PAC works to identify and cultivate relationships with promising recruits for elected office. The SFAA PAC also supports ballot initiatives which benefit property owners, while also working in conjunction with other Political Action Committees and organizations to oppose ballot measures and tax increases which are harmful for property owners.

statements.kind: voter guide on the organisation's own site
statements.section: Prop D - Changes to Ballot Measure Process
statements.text: We recommend voting Yes on D. We support this measure because San Francisco's current ballot measure system is flawed and results in overly long ballots in which residents are asked to vote on a wide variety of measures that can be quite complex in nature.

statements.kind: voter guide on the organisation's own site
statements.section: Prop E - City Administrator's Authority and Changes to City Contracting
statements.text: We recommend voting Yes on E. This charter amendment makes critical reforms to our City government's contracting system.

statements.kind: voter guide on the organisation's own site
statements.section: Prop F - Changes to Executive Branch Management
statements.text: We recommend voting Yes on F. This charter amendment makes much-needed changes to SF's government structure as recommended both by 2023's Rose Report (sponsored by our predecessor organization TogetherSF) and by good government think tank SPUR.

statements.kind: voter guide on the organisation's own site
statements.section: Prop H - Parcel Tax to Fund Public Muni Operations
statements.text: We recommend voting No on H. Transit is important. But so is everything the city provides -that doesn't mean we keep charging taxpayers more instead of fixing the city budget.

statements.kind: voter guide on the organisation's own site
statements.section: Prop I - Changes to Real Property Transfer Tax
statements.text: We recommend voting No on I. This measure moves General Fund money into an earmarked fund, which means the city loses flexibility to use those dollars where they're needed most, like covering budget shortfalls.

statements.kind: voter guide on the organisation's own site
statements.section: Prop J - Removal of Foreclosure Exemption for Real Property Transfer Tax
statements.text: We recommend voting No on J. Originally, this measure was supposed to be paired with a reduction in the real transfer tax to be part of a revenue-neutral package. But now that it's not, all this measure does is raise taxes, hampering Downtown's recovery.
